1: Six numbers make a traveller. Strength carries the pack, Constitution fills out the body, Dexterity slips the blow, Intelligence deepens the well of magic, Wisdom slows the clock, and Perception sees a little farther.
Wisdom is time. Every point of it is one more second to think while something is trying to eat you.
The dungeon is a harsh teacher but an honest one. Go deeper than you have ever been and you arrive a little wiser.
What does a sword care how strong your arm is? It cares whether you can add.
One right answer lands a blow. A string of them, unbroken, lands a far heavier one.
Get the very first sum wrong and you have swung at the air. Get a later one wrong and you still keep what you built.
Nobody makes you answer until the clock runs dry. When the thing in front of you is nearly dead, strike and be done.
Know the beast and you know where the meat is. The butcher's question is always about the animal.
A carcass is not a cut of meat, and a cut of meat is not a supper. One question stands between each.
Nobody down here ever grew tough by fighting. They grew tough at supper. Cook a meal properly and the body keeps a little of it for good.
Wands ask how the world works. Answer, and the world does as it is told.
Written magic is fussy about grammar. Read it wrongly and it is only paper.
Nothing down here wears its true name. Philosophy is the art of asking a thing what it really is.
Prayer is help that actually comes. How much of it comes depends on how well you know the old stories.
Armor remembers where it was made. Know your way around the world and it will let you put it on.
Every ring has a past. It will not sit on a finger that knows no history.
To a thief a lock is only a price. Understand what things cost and most lids come open.
Each step costs a crumb, and so does each moment spent standing still. When the crumbs run out the dungeon starts taking them out of you.
The question mark is the wisest key on the board. Press it whenever the dungeon stops making sense.
Treasure does not leap into packs. Stand on it and stoop.
Some hides shrug at an edge and split under a hammer. Carry more than one kind of argument.
Look at what a monster is made of before you choose what to hit it with. Things of ice and things of fire seldom enjoy each other's company.
No charm against fire makes you fireproof. It makes you half as sorry.
From a dead adventurer's journal: 'Rested an hour. Feel better. Hungry. Something is coming down the corridor.'
Stand quietly for long enough and the mind refills, a drop at a time. It will not work with something chewing on you.
New stairs put a little wind back in your lungs. The same stairs twice put back nothing.
Floors never announce their traps. A sharp eye, passing close, sometimes does it for them.
Loot belongs to its floor. If you want better treasure there is only one direction to go, and it is not up.
Plain boxes hold a plain handful. The handsomer the chest, the more is inside it, and the worse it bites a clumsy thief.
Each floor pays a little better than the one above it, and anything worth buying costs a fair piece of a floor. Count your purse the way a shopkeeper would.
Whatever question beats you today will be asked again. Next time you will know it, and that is the one treasure the dungeon cannot take back.
You should know better than to pick up a duck in a dungeon.
Fountains ask before they give. Answer well and the water is kind. Answer badly and you will wish you had stayed thirsty.
Whatever the dead loved is buried with them. Dig only if you know your way around a map, and are ready for the owner to object.
An empty throne judges whoever sits on it, and it judges by how much of the past they know.
Listen when you arrive somewhere new. Someone counting coins behind a wall is not a ghost story. It is directions.
There is a small grey trader on the deep roads with a pack twice his size. Stand beside him and ask to see inside it.
A trader buys as well as sells, though never for more than a fraction of his own price. Name a thing before you sell it and he will pay a little more.
Rust and acid take an edge, not forever. A smith with a file can give back what the wet took.
Somebody always sets up shop on the last floor before a great beast's lair. Heroes pay best the night before a fight.
A trader's price says something about what is in the bottle, if you have the eye to read it.
Merchants talk to merchants. Rob one and the rest will know your face.
The monks who drew the bonnacon gave it horns that curl backwards and can hurt nobody. Then they drew the knight running from its other end.
Saint Brendan once said Mass on an island that swam away. A pilgrim who can find himself on a chart has less to fear from solid ground.
The poorest table in the dungeon is the one most worth sitting at. Do not come to it empty-handed.
A promise made in the dark is still a promise. The ones you carry all the way down are remembered at the bottom; the ones you sell are remembered longer.
Not everyone who weeps in chains was chained unjustly. Mercy that never asks a single question is only a kind of hurry.
A purse is never lighter than just after a stranger brushes past. A thief who runs is a thief who can be caught, and the dead pay all their debts.
2: Something is asleep inside the small ivory sphere. Throw it gently. You do not get to choose who wakes up.
A companion that fights beside you long enough stops being the creature you first met.
Hurt companions mend slowly by themselves. They mend faster on your supper, and faster still on your medicine.
You may tell a companion to follow, to hold its ground, or to go hunting. It will not guess which one you wanted.
Feed a companion from your own pack and it grows faster than fighting alone would make it. Your stomach will notice the difference.
Companions fight as well as their master has been answering. Your mistakes make them clumsy too.
The little shard of the Stone is how you question a thing. Lose it and everything stays a stranger.
Guess at a thing's true name and guess wrong, and the shard will leave you seeing stars. Never do your philosophy with a monster watching.
Things come blessed, plain or cursed, and they do not say which. The cursed ones are easy to put on.
Lay a thing on an altar and it may confess what it is. The altar tells the truth to the kind, lies to the cruel, and says nothing to those who are neither.
Wands run dry, scrolls burn up, and a spellbook goes on teaching for as long as you go on listening.
Mana is a well, and a clever head digs it deeper. Do not draw the last bucket for something small.
Prayers are answered as far as you can carry them. The first right answer brings a little. The last brings a great deal.
Pray anywhere and you are heard. Pray at an altar and you are heard one step further.
There are two things worth asking for on your knees: mercy for the body, or a steadier hand for the fight. Heaven answers the one you asked.
Heaven is generous but never hurried. After one prayer is answered it is a long walk before the next one will be.
Besides ordinary prayer there is one great plea, and Heaven hears it a single time. Make it at an altar, or be very sure of your theology.
Nothing done in the dark is hidden from Heaven. How you treat the helpless on the way down is waiting for you near the bottom.
Carry a spare loaf and a spare potion. Somebody down there will need them more than you do, and it is noticed when you agree.
When a stranger names a price down here, it is no longer pocket change. Decide what the thing is worth before you open your purse.
Perception does not find traps from across the room. It finds them just before your foot does, which is the distance that matters.
Clever hands can do better than break a trap. They can change its mind about whom it is for.
Some dishes are only supper. Others leave something of the beast in the cook, for an hour or for good.
Two things eaten are two snacks. Two things cooked together may be a recipe nobody wrote down.
The pot asks one question. Get it right and you have dinner. Get it wrong and you have smoke.
How much the kitchen can do for you depends on how deep you have dared to go. A cook who stays near the top stays small.
Before it opens, a chest wants one answer about money. A wrong one opens something else.
The trader's first price is only where the talking starts. Each good argument knocks a slice off, and he will hear you out once for each thing he sells.
Fountains, graves and thrones give most to those who answer longest. The very last answer buys something you keep.
A wrong answer does not undo the right ones before it. The chain stops where it stood, and the blow falls anyway.
Learn a whole shelf of history and the dungeon stops quizzing you on it. Sums are different. The sword never takes your word for it.
Blades ask the sums of their metal. Soft metal asks a child's questions. What the deep smiths forged asks a scholar's, and hits far harder for the trouble.
Armor from deep down asks about farther lands. A helm you cannot answer for is only a heavy hat.
Silver for what ought to be dead, cold iron for the fair folk. The old wives were right about metals.
Whatever lands on the shield is a blow you never have to heal.
Armor is an argument, not a wall. Even the best of it loses now and then.
Scratched low on a wall, in a shaky hand: 'The vine does not chase you. It did not need to.'
Every so often the dungeon stops being rooms and becomes a maze. Every so often after that, the stairs have an owner.
To see a monster is not to know it. Its body will tell you everything, if you know how to ask.
Those who die down here do not always leave. Some stay to guard what they were carrying, and they do not recognise old friends.
This dungeon has had famous visitors before you. It still remembers their names, and it is polite to anyone who arrives wearing one.
Give a great name at the door and you may be greeted as that hero. The door wants the whole name, and it checks the spelling.
I know I shouldn't pick up that duck... but what if...
Certain altars want a gift before they will listen, and the gift is never far. Search the other rooms before you give up.
Somewhere in the upper dungeon grows a carrot far too good to eat. Whoever it is meant for is waiting further down.
An alchemist's crucible wants lead before it will part with gold, and it likes a little philosophy while it works.
The Welsh said a certain cauldron would not boil a coward's food. The one down here is less particular, so long as you bring it enough dishes.
Nicholas of Myra threw his gold through a window at night so that nobody could thank him. The ledger of gifts marks the unsigned ones.
Lions remember longer than men do. Androcles found that out in front of all Rome.
The Watch never stops waiting for a dispatch. A sealed case is dead weight only until it meets the right sergeant.
The quick are missed more often than the armored are spared. Past a point, nimble feet do what no more plate can.
Some purses are held out so that someone can watch you take them. Turning down a thing you could have taken, because taking it would be wrong, is seen even when nobody is looking.
Helping is not the same as being good. A kindness given blind can cost you dearly, and buys nothing on the scales.
Not every cold spot is a draught. When a blow comes out of empty air, walk into the air, and you will find what threw it.
Some slimes are only multiplied by a sword. Ask what the blade will make before you swing it.
3: Companions grow by time at your side, by its kills, by being fed, and by being made a fuss of. No single one of these will do.
After its first great change a companion learns a trick of its own. You will find it listed beside its name.
A companion called back into its sphere is not gone. Throw the sphere again and the same friend steps out, name and all.
Watch where your companion will not step. It can smell a curse lying on the floor, and you cannot.
One question unmasks a thing completely: its name, its curse, its strength and its story. There is no second question to hide behind.
Name one potion and you have named all its sisters. Whether a particular bottle is blessed or cursed is still its own secret.
Spells have shapes: a line, a fan, a burst. Know which one you are holding before you decide where to stand.
Two enemies fighting each other are two fewer fighting you. There is magic that arranges it.
Only so much building can be done on a body in one place. A few good meals on a floor do all the good that twenty would.
Food can raise a gift of the body only so high, and the ceiling lifts as you descend. Feast near the top and most of it is wasted.
Some powers live in no wand and no book. They live in the hero, and wait in a small menu until they are called.
A hero's own power asks questions no sword or pot ever asks. The further you answer, the larger the gift.
Great deeds are not a daily habit. Use your power and expect to finish the floor without it.
Take a trap apart perfectly and it gives up more than its spring. The dungeon pays its best tinkers in secrets.
A rewired trap is loyal exactly once.
Mercy arrives in a fixed order: strength first, then healing, then the mind, then what you carry, and last of all a shield. How far down the list you get is up to you.
Ask the Archangel to guide your hand and what he lends is time. Carry the prayer the whole way and the clock runs twice as long, for a few blows.
Heaven hears a whisper from the bottom of a well better than a shout from the top of a tower.
From clean hands the same prayer is worth more. At an altar the difference doubles, for good and for ill.
No single deed is weighed at the bottom. The whole road is. Start early.
Plain metals come first, and after them metals with names out of stories. When a weapon's sums suddenly turn hard, look again at what it is made of.
The horned king walks through the walls of his own maze, which is hardly fair. A princess of Crete once handed a stranger something small that made it fair. It was not a sword.
No blade could pierce the lion Heracles strangled. Whoever wears its hide feels half of every blow, which is half more than the lion ever did.
Golden thread seems a poor thing to carry into a monster's house. Ask Theseus what he would have paid for a second spool.
Minos owed the sea a bull and kept it. A bronze one in your pack is the same debt, and it can still be paid in water.
Asterion forgives a traveller who never learned to cook. Nothing below him does.
Her gaze crosses a whole hall, but it cannot go round a corner. Count the pillars before you count on your courage.
Three old sisters shared one eye between them and lost it. It is no use for seeing with. Returned to the right hands, it is a great deal of use.
Perseus carried his polished shield on his arm. He would have looked a fool with it strapped to his luggage.
Medusa cannot harm what cannot see her. A strip of cloth is a desperate answer, and it is still an answer.
No quest for a great stair is finished on the floor where it begins. Carry strange things downward. Somebody below is waiting for them.
Each great stair has an owner with a name, and each name comes with an old story about how the owner died. Read the story before you knock.
Any gatekeeper can be beaten the hard way. About half of those who try it are available for comment.
Shovels make poor weapons, until something heavy walks across what they dug.
Sigurd did not think of the pit by himself. An old one-eyed stranger did. Take your advice from the same quarter.
Every creature you have truly studied has a page in your book, and the page says what hurts it. Read before you sharpen.
The dungeon notices habits: one weapon kept faithfully, one mistake survived again and again, one prayer made at every threshold. Enough of any habit earns it a name.
Not everyone you meet down here is selling the same thing. Some sell goods, some sell stories, and some are buying you.
When a bargain feels too rich at the moment it is offered, ask who profits if you say yes.
Find something that plainly belonged to someone, and you may expect to meet the someone a little further down.
Burdens taken up for a stranger cannot always be set down again. An altar can break what hands cannot.
Fire, poison and an open wound all charge the same toll, and it is a share of you, not a fixed fee. The bigger you grow, the more they cost.
There are touches that take a piece of you supper will not put back. A strong body throws them off more often than a weak one.
A rattled head still knows the answer. It just has less time to say it.
With your wits scrambled, the sums come no slower but the clock runs out sooner. Answer what you are sure of first.
Healing draughts mend a share of you, not a fixed amount. They are worth as much at the bottom as at the top.
Clear a floor and it does not stay cleared. Something always wanders in to see what the noise was.
Read the first line you are given on a new floor. Sometimes it is a warning about who lives there, and it never uses their name.
They say the duck is a tutor in patience. Nobody who finished the lesson was ever seen without it.
The box that says 'Do not open' has a very good lock on it. Hope was never found by anyone who picked it cleanly.
Odin paid for his drink at the well before he tasted it, and nobody offered him the eye back.
Percival sat at the wounded king's table and was too polite to ask what ailed him. He was not invited twice.
The Sphinx of the deep is more patient than her sister at Thebes. She asks several riddles, each harder than the last, but she forgives no wrong answer.
One missed stroke of the bellows spoils a dwarf-smith's work. The unfinished hammer-head wants somebody who can keep count.
A king's seal found loose in the dungeon opens no door. It earns a hearing before an empty judgment seat, and the questions there are about the past.
The Fleece hung in a grove at Colchis under a serpent that never slept. It is beasts the serpent wants to hear about.
In a roofless chapel there is a bare altar with a ring worn into the stone where a cup once stood. Bring the cup, and know your scripture.
No one walks up to a unicorn. Stand where she can see you, keep still, and let her decide.
She has never taken food from a hand. The ground near her is good enough.
Unicorns know what kind of traveller is standing in front of them. The cruel do not get a second look.
There is no cow level. Anyone who tells you otherwise has been bothering livestock, and not just the once.
Blades skidded off the Boar of Calydon. Atalanta's arrow went in, and Meleager's spear after it. The spear was kept.
In Utgard the contests are never what they look like. Thor lost all three, and frightened his host badly by how nearly he won.
You are what you eat. Before you cook the beast, ask what the beast was good at.
One good meal is a promise. A second, a floor later, is the promise kept.
Stillness refills the mind, but each floor holds only so much quiet. Deeper down there is more.
A spell is a lever, not a hammer. Use it to move the fight, then finish the fight with your own arithmetic.
Nerve is not a single brave moment. Hold firm when the hard questions come, and hold firm again a long way further down; it is the second time that shows what you are.
Give a stranger what he asks before you know what he is, and you may pay for it in blood, in coin, or in someone else's grief.
The one-eyed giant and the many-eyed horror see what is really there. Eat as they saw, and for a while so will you.
Elisha's servant saw nothing until his eyes were opened, and then the hills were full of chariots. Some draughts open eyes a little way.
Men who grew from dragon's teeth trust nobody, not even each other. A stone thrown among them is a fine argument.
4: A companion is offered a name the moment it wakes. The name goes with it into the sphere and comes back out again.
Legends do not answer to easy philosophy. The harder a thing was to make, the harder the question that unmasks it.
One philosopher wrote that what does not kill him makes him stronger. Down here he meant it exactly: the lower his blood, the harder his hand.
His mother dipped him in the river and missed one spot. Enter under his name and your skin sheds a part of every blow.
A white-haired monster-hunter was remade as a boy to resist flame and venom. He hits everything a little harder for it, too.
When the world closes around the last of the Elder Blood, she steps sideways and is somewhere else. Cornering her is a waste of an afternoon.
One Athenian needs no shard to see what a thing is. He looks past the thing to its idea.
Curses are wasted on the Cynic of Sinope. He owns nothing and wants nothing, and to a man who does not care, a cursed ring is only a ring.
Ithaca's king never trusted the strongest sword. He trusts the right word at the right moment, and for a while his enemy fights for him.
Two swords are better than one, said the Sword Saint, and he wrote a book to prove it. His way was learned far from here. Steel does not mind.
When the Maid of Domremy raises her white banner, wounds close and the next blow lands half again as hard.
To the detective of Baker Street the dungeon is a problem in want of attention. He glances round a room and tells you what is in it.
In Vinci there once lived a man whose notebooks were full of helpers he never built. Down here, for a little while, one of them gets up and walks.
Rome scourged the queen of the Iceni and lived to regret it. Hurt her badly enough and she answers in a fury.
To the first programmer, every monster is a procedure. Procedures can be paused.
Viriditas was the abbess of Bingen's word for the greenness in living things. Where she calls it down, wounds close and sickness lets go.
One inventor was more lightning than man. Whatever strikes him in anger gets a little of it back.
Whoever borrows the Titan's stolen fire pays for it as he does: a little, every time, out of his own body.
A king of Sparta plants his feet and will not be moved. While he stands, blows glance off him and some of them come straight back.
Whole armies ran from the boy-king of Macedon. Ordinary monsters still do. The owners of the great stairs only laugh.
Thrice-great, they called the messenger who does not walk through a dungeon but steps around it. The better he answers, the longer the step.
Give the Stagirite a good answer and half your pack tells him its name at once. Sorting the world into kinds was always his trade.
Athens once had a man who could question a crowd until it no longer knew its own mind. It works on guards. It never worked on judges.
On Samos a sage taught that the world is tuned like a string. Pluck it rightly and a body comes back into tune.
Whoever killed the first Minotaur remembers how a maze wants to be walked. Ask him well and the whole floor lies open.
An old enchanter who once raised a king can call down a star. Small things are flattened by it. Great ones feel only half.
Hephaestus once wove a net fine enough to catch a god of war. Lesser things caught in it mostly stand and stare.
From the haunted mere came an old blade that forgives one slip of the tongue on every floor. Only one.
Odin's spear has never missed what it was thrown at. It is not about to start on your account.
Endings feed the jackal-god's black sickle. Each life it finishes puts a little back into the hand that holds it.
Four kinds sleep in the common spheres: one of sparks, one of water, one of thorns and one of flame. Almost always.
Very rarely, the wolf who will one day swallow the sun has come to heel. Never for anyone who found him by the stairs.
Answer the unicorn perfectly and she does more than bless you. She comes along, and she is a better doctor than a fighter.
The hero who killed the dragon did not meet it standing up.
Dragon fire passes over the head of anyone low enough. So does the dragon's patience: he will come looking.
Lay a broken sword on Odin's altar and he will take it politely and give you something to dig with. He once claimed a whole army by throwing a spear over it. He respects the gesture.
A dead dragon's blood is worth drinking, if you know your beasts. The more of the birds' talk you can follow, the more they tell you.
Perseus kept only the head. A good cook might keep rather more, and never fear that kind of stare again.
The wolf grows angrier the longer he is fought. The gods never beat him by strength. They used a ribbon once, and they are keeping a shoe for later.
From a journal found frozen shut: 'He cannot keep his feet on the ice. Why did I fight him on the stone?'
Dwarves bound the wolf with things that do not exist: the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain. Somebody has been leaving them about.
Each thing the ribbon needs announces itself as you arrive on its floor. The dungeon is not usually so helpful. Take the hint.
On the dwarves' anvil there is a cup for each thing it needs. It will tell you how many are still empty, and it will not start early.
Binding the wolf is not free, even with the ribbon. Tyr paid a hand for it. You will pay something smaller, each time.
Scraps that cobblers throw away go into the silent god's shoe, which has been a very long time in the making. It was never meant for walking in.
Old cobblers swear that every scrap cut from a shoe goes somewhere. The first lies very near the top of the dungeon. Keep it, and keep counting.
Close above the wolf, the silent god keeps an altar with a cobbler's last on it. It wants leather, and it can count.
Somewhere below lies a worn page in red-brown ink that smells of old fires. It is one verse long. Keep it until you understand whom the verse is about.
An ancient tablet with a hollow in its centre is half of something. The other half is not found until the very end, and it shines.
Hell's princes each keep a seal and a stair. Neither opens while its keeper lives, and the last stair of all counts every one.
No two of the seal-keepers fight alike. One grows wrathful once he bleeds, one feeds on the wounds he gives, one never stands still. Learn each before you close with him.
Below the wolf, certain floors have a legend living on them and others do not. The stair will tell you which as you step off it.
Scratched beside a stair, far down: 'The scales give nothing to a soul that weighs nothing either way. The lukewarm go on unarmed.'
Only prayer wakes the altar of the scales, and it wakes once.
An Archangel's scales weigh souls, and can do one other thing. Whoever carries them into the last hall does not fight alone.
When the scales call, the Host of Heaven comes, and fights only locusts: one angel for each.
No one finds the blade of white fire. It is given, and only to those who reach the bottom having kept their word, refused what was not theirs, and held firm the whole way down.
Your old self may be waiting on the floor where it fell, guarding your old gear. The gear has gone bad. So has the owner.
Certain altars are not for praying at. Each asks one thing, once. Walking away is free. A wrong answer is not.
Sisyphus left his boulder at the foot of a slope. Take it up and walk. The hill counts every step you carry it.
A guildhall ledger, half burned: 'Bearer of the duck, a very great many turns; rewarded.' The line after it is ash.
Over a smoking rift sits a priestess who takes coin and answers in riddles about the habits the dungeon rewards. She is cheaper than learning them by accident.
Holy books are worth a blessing to the right hands and a purse of gold to the wrong ones. Whoever carries one is asked, on the way down, which kind of hands he has.
A sealed scroll taken from a named terror is worth more above ground than below. It is meant for a father's eyes.
Jerome kept a lion under his desk and a skull on top of it, and held that a translator who dodges a hard word has told a lie.
A wounded king left alone does not stay wounded. If you walk away from a throne room, expect to start again.
The bull does not tire. He gets angrier. Whatever you mean to do to him, do it quickly.
A clever mind does not make the fire hotter. It makes the fire last, and reach the far side of the room.
Fortune will hand you a few gifts and then close her hand. What you cook and what you choose, she cannot take back.
The scales do not tally every good deed. Each long stretch of the descent is weighed once, so a heap of virtue in one place counts for less than goodness carried the whole way down.
A promise you simply fail to keep is not a lie, and is not punished as one. But it is not a promise kept, and the long count knows the difference.
A floor has one way down. When you count two, one of them is hungry.
Medusa had two sisters, and neither of them can die for long. Bring the mirror and the blindfold twice.
5: The Stone waits at the very bottom, in the keeping of the last enemy. Getting it is half the errand. The other half is every stair you came down, in reverse.
Half of every blow is swallowed by the dark the Destroyer stands in. Light is the cure for dark, and in that hall there is light to be had for the asking.

A ring of altars stands round the last hall. Each will burn for one prayer, however lately you prayed. The fire strips the dark from the Destroyer, but only for a few breaths, so have your sums ready.
White fire does not notice the Destroyer's darkness, and it hates the things of the Pit above all others. Few arrive carrying that blade. The rest must find their light on the spot.
There are three roads through the last dark: borrowed fire, a given sword, or plain stubbornness. The third is by far the longest.
His locusts rise as fast as they fall, up to a limit, and the limit is higher for the wicked. The Destroyer never fights alone for long.
A wounded Destroyer is worse than a whole one. Keep something back for the end of the fight.
The Destroyer is weighed before he is fought. What the scales found on the floor above decides how strong he is and how many he brings.
Just above the bottom you are weighed, by the Archangel whose name is on the white blade. He has been watching since the first floor.
Honour and cruelty are paid at the bottom in the same coin. Those who kept faith all the way down are armed for the last fight. The cruel find the last fight has been armed against them.
Between the sword and the sentence the Archangel keeps several other verdicts. You choose yours one stranger at a time.
No saint was ever made in a hurry. The honest road through the dungeon is the expensive one, floor after floor.
Breaking a seal has nothing to do with touching it. Seals break when their keepers fall.
Truly unkillable things do not exist down here. The songs give every such creature a heel, and the dungeon has kept the songs.
Death is not waiting at the bottom. He sets out when the Stone starts upward: slow in the deep, quicker with every stretch of the climb, and near the surface faster than you.
Last page of a climber's journal: 'His speed buys him distance, not blows. The scythe only falls on those who stop beside him. I have stopped to write this down.'
Prayer cannot kill Death. It can make him wait, and at an altar he waits longer.
Stop time if you have the means. One traveller on the stairs behind you will not notice.
Ending Death takes a place, a tool, a verse and a tablet, and the dungeon hands them out in that order on the way down. The first means nothing when you meet it.
On one of the early floors the ground shimmers and quotes a verse at whoever stands there. Nothing happens. Remember the place anyway.
A Stone of legend and a Tablet of legend are two halves of one key, and neither knows it. Something very ordinary from a workman's belt introduces them.
The last book says what finally becomes of Death. One scroll down here carries the line. It matters a great deal where the reader is standing, and who is standing there with him.
Only one place lets Death be ended, and it lies near the top, which is also where he runs fastest. Arrive with the work already done.
Long before this dungeon, a cave game hid one nonsense word that carried the player somewhere else. People have been typing it into things ever since. It still works.
Not every key does what it says on it. A few seem to do nothing at all. One of those is only waiting for you to finish the sentence.

Speak the hidden word and it asks questions of its own, about thinking machines of all things. The first right answer mends you. Each one after gives a gift that is given only once, and the last has teeth.
Reality does not enjoy being rewritten and needs a long rest afterwards. Save the word for real trouble.
There are subjects no weapon, pot or prayer will ever ask you. One is for remembering lore. The other belongs to traps, fountains and the powers of heroes, and it is about the minds of machines.
One great plea, answered once and finally. From an altar the question is gentle. From anywhere else there are several, and none of them is.
Heaven does not take a careless great plea kindly. Ask afterwards what you are wearing, if you can still see it.
Name enough things truly and the naming begins to change the namer: first a quicker mind, later a sharper eye, and at the very last something to wear. The count is long. Start early.
A companion changes its whole shape twice in a life. The first change takes many floors of company. The second, most companions never live to see.
Not every name the door knows comes out of an old book. A monster-hunter with a silver sword, a lost princess, a shop clerk with a short temper: the dungeon has read widely.
Thor's belt of strength gives its wearer what the songs promise, and makes him quicker into the bargain.
A boy from a small town who meant to be the very best wears a cap that makes companions grow faster. The door knows him by his full name.
Odin's arm-ring dripped eight new rings every ninth night. The one down here is less generous. It makes the arm that wears it stronger, and gold seems to find that arm.
Andvari's ring was cursed to ruin every owner it ever had. The one down here has mellowed. It helps its owner notice what is hidden, and what is hidden is often gold.
By the bottom you will have several times the thinking time you began with. Every second of it will be spoken for.
Rest will close a wound, but only so far. The last of your strength comes back at the table, in a bottle, or on your knees.
A hint is a riddle, not a recipe. The dungeon trusts you to do the rest of the work.
When the well of lore runs dry, let it fill. Memory, like any spring, wants a while between buckets.
If two hints seem to quarrel, they are probably talking about different travellers. The dungeon is large enough for both.
Wear the duck. Endure it. Speak softly to it. The dungeon's jokes are not all at your expense. Some of them just take a very long time to land.
The same right thing done once is a good day. Done again, and again, stretch after stretch, it becomes a character, and character is what the Archangel weighs.
Kindness without judgment is a coin tossed into the dark. Look first, ask first, then give: the careful hand is the one the scales remember.
A small cut makes two of what bleeds salt. One great blow makes none.
Deep down there are jaws that weigh the heart before they bite. Keep yours light.
